doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

chapter: Sessions and teaching in New Orleans
title: Choosing teaching over full-time performing
summary: Jordan chose education, has taught and played all his life with seven kids, and tells students to get a degree; he drifted into R&B work as second tier behind the top New Orleans session players.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Was there a point where you decided, okay I’m going to be a musician. I’m going to make a living as a musician?

Well there was a point where I decided I was going to be an educator when I went to college. Now all through my college days I played in them bands with leaders or somebody would say I could make a gig, and when I finished college I got a teaching job my first year out and so I’ve been teaching and playing all my life. I’ve never made a living as a professional musician, because I got seven kids.
That formula was not going to work.

That’s right. And that’s what I tell all the young kids now. You know they say, “I want to be a musician, I’m going to New York, I’m going to do this.” I say, “man, get your degree so at least you can have something to fall back on.” And I wasn’t never in the thing of being a professional musician, my whole thing was teaching and all the gigs and things on the side. And I had too many of them on the side because after I got out of school I started playing in rhythm & blues. Rock & roll was just coming on, so I started playing in some of them, and Fats Domino and them had been the studio or Dave Bartholomew and rock was beginning to really go. And everybody was coming to New Orleans to record. So in the first tier, like Red Tyler and Lee Allen and all of them, they’d be in the studio all day and half of the night, then we could take it at midnight until in the morning. You understand? We were the second tier.
